voice.refText: You wake up and discover you can pause time. 10 seconds once a day. At first, you use it for dumb things. You catch your falling coffee. You dodge your boss in the hallway.

Nurse.describe: A low, brisk female alto: a clinic nurse in her forties at the end of a night shift. Dry and kind, practical, crisp clear diction, every word distinct, standard American English.

Broker.describe: A smooth male baritone: a salesman in a grey suit in his fifties. Unhurried and friendly, a little too calm, every word a quiet offer, crisp clear diction, every word distinct.

Brother.describe: A light, bright male tenor: a boy of about eighteen in his last year of school, the listener's younger brother. Quick, teasing and wry, warm underneath, crisp clear diction, every word distinct, casual modern American English.

Bridge woman.describe: A clear, warm female voice, a woman in her forties. Mezzo, natural and conversational.

Boss.describe: A cheerful male baritone: an office boss in his late forties. Hearty and pleased with himself, brisk, a grin in the voice, crisp clear diction, every word distinct.

Grandmother.describe: A bright female voice, an old soprano: a grandmother in her eighties next door. Delighted with herself, slow and satisfied, clear diction, every word distinct, a light Mexican Spanish accent.

Clerk.describe: A flat, deep male baritone: a warehouse door clerk in his thirties. Bored and blunt, short words, crisp clear diction, every word distinct.

lines.text: Nurse: That's all the plasma we can take this week. Come back Thursday.
lines.say: [plain and kind, clear, a small stress on all and on Thursday] That's all the plasma we can take this week. Come back Thursday.
lines.speaker: Nurse

lines.text: Broker: You fell asleep for ten seconds, and you earned a coin.
lines.say: [easy, amused, a little pause after seconds, a stress on earned] You fell asleep for ten seconds, and you earned a coin.
lines.speaker: Broker

lines.text: Broker: Wear this tonight. Sleep all night, and get paid for every hour.
lines.say: [smooth, unhurried, a pause after tonight, stresses on all night and every hour] Wear this tonight. Sleep all night, and get paid for every hour.
lines.speaker: Broker

lines.text: Twice a week, you sell your plasma, the pale part of your blood. It's the most the law allows.
lines.say: [low, plain, close to the ear, a stress on plasma, a short pause before It's the most] Twice a week, you sell your plasma, the pale part of your blood. It's the most the law allows.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It's how your family keeps up with what it owes.
lines.say: [quiet, a little heavy, a stress on family and owes] It's how your family keeps up with what it owes.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So what if a company could rent your brain while you slept?
lines.say: [curious, leaning in, the question offered like a coin] So what if a company could rent your brain while you slept?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: That's the band. A thin strip you wear across your forehead.
lines.say: [clear, slow, presenting it, a stress on band, a pause after it] That's the band. A thin strip you wear across your forehead.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: While you sleep, it lends your brain to a company. And it pays you, by the hour.
lines.say: [clear, explaining, a stress on lends your brain, a pause before And it pays you, a stress on by the hour] While you sleep, it lends your brain to a company. And it pays you, by the hour.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Midnight. The band goes on. A chime.
lines.say: [hushed, three short beats with air between them] Midnight. The band goes on. A chime.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: That pale figure up there? That's your sleeping brain, at work for the company.
lines.say: [curious on the question, then plain, a stress on sleeping brain] That pale figure up there? That's your sleeping brain, at work for the company.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You feel nothing. But a night you sell is a night your own brain doesn't get.
lines.say: [quiet, a pause after nothing, then slow and cold, a stress on own] You feel nothing. But a night you sell is a night your own brain doesn't get.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: What'd you get?
lines.say: [bright, teasing, shaking a jar] What'd you get?
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: Brother: Scam.
lines.say: [flat, certain, one word] Scam.
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: Ninety dollars. For eight hours of lying down. The best wage of your life. And that's the problem.
lines.say: [dry, a smile on the wage, then the smile gone on the last sentence] Ninety dollars. For eight hours of lying down. The best wage of your life. And that's the problem.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Because you count every waking hour as money you did or didn't earn. And nobody's ever paid you for one asleep.
lines.say: [warm, knowing, a little sad on the second sentence] Because you count every waking hour as money you did or didn't earn. And nobody's ever paid you for one asleep.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The band came with a leaflet. It sets out the deal.
lines.say: [clear, brisk, a stress on leaflet and on deal] The band came with a leaflet. It sets out the deal.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Wear the band to bed. While you sleep, the company runs its work on your brain.
lines.say: [plain, step by step, a pause after bed, a stress on your brain] Wear the band to bed. While you sleep, the company runs its work on your brain.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And every morning, the band pays you, by the hour.
lines.say: [light, a stress on pays you, the last words slow] And every morning, the band pays you, by the hour.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You won't feel a thing. One company can link many bands, for one big job.
lines.say: [measured, a pause after thing, a stress on many bands and one big job] You won't feel a thing. One company can link many bands, for one big job.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But the leaflet promises each brain stays separate. One brain, one band, one jar.
lines.say: [slow, a stress on promises and separate, then each of the three short phrases its own beat] But the leaflet promises each brain stays separate. One brain, one band, one jar.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And you won't remember the work. Only small leftovers. The leaflet calls them crumbs: a taste, a word, a face that isn't yours.
lines.say: [measured, a pause after work, a stress on crumbs, the list slow] And you won't remember the work. Only small leftovers. The leaflet calls them crumbs: a taste, a word, a face that isn't yours.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It says they're harmless.
lines.say: [light, a hint of doubt on harmless] It says they're harmless.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Why would anyone want a sleeping brain? The leaflet explains that too.
lines.say: [curious, a real question, a pause after it] Why would anyone want a sleeping brain? The leaflet explains that too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Your brain burns about twenty watts. At night, the leaflet calls that unused power.
lines.say: [plain, a stress on twenty watts, then the salesman's phrase unused power half-mocked] Your brain burns about twenty watts. At night, the leaflet calls that unused power.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It's true. In 2022, brain cells in a dish, wired to the old bat-and-ball video game, began to get better at it within five minutes. So a whole brain for eight hours is a bargain.
lines.say: [amazed, a little delighted on it's true, then dry on the bargain] It's true. In 2022, brain cells in a dish, wired to the old bat-and-ball video game, began to get better at it within five minutes. So a whole brain for eight hours is a bargain.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: Still a scam.
lines.say: [mouth full, unimpressed] Still a scam.
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: He reads the leaflet upside down. And by Saturday he's wearing one.
lines.say: [fond, amused, the second sentence a wink] He reads the leaflet upside down. And by Saturday he's wearing one.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Morning two. You wake craving a food you can't name. So you draw it for him.
lines.say: [light, quick, a story beginning] Morning two. You wake craving a food you can't name. So you draw it for him.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: That's a shoe.
lines.say: [deadpan, head tilted] That's a shoe.
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: Morning three. You hum a tune in the shower that nobody has written. The grandmother next door bangs on the wall.
lines.say: [amused, a little mischievous, the bang in the voice] Morning three. You hum a tune in the shower that nobody has written. The grandmother next door bangs on the wall.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then she hums it back. Note for note. Through the wall.
lines.say: [slow, surprised, a chill under the smile] Then she hums it back. Note for note. Through the wall.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Morning four. You fold a fitted sheet into a perfect square. His spoon hits the floor.
lines.say: [brisk, deadpan, the spoon landing dry] Morning four. You fold a fitted sheet into a perfect square. His spoon hits the floor.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Morning five. You know the word for bridge in a language you've never heard. So you try it on the woman at the bridge, the one who crosses twice a week to sell her plasma too.
lines.say: [curious, quick, warmer on the woman] Morning five. You know the word for bridge in a language you've never heard. So you try it on the woman at the bridge, the one who crosses twice a week to sell her plasma too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Bridge woman: Not mine.
lines.say: [tired, a shrug, not unkind] Not mine.
lines.speaker: Bridge woman

lines.text: She shrugs. She doesn't know it either. So whose is it?
lines.say: [quiet, a question left in the air] She shrugs. She doesn't know it either. So whose is it?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Saturday. Your brother, palm out. And a teal light under his cap.
lines.say: [fond, a beat before the light, caught-you in the voice] Saturday. Your brother, palm out. And a teal light under his cap.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: Okay. What'd you get?
lines.say: [bright, curious, crisp and clear, a stress on what'd] Okay. What'd you get?
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: Breakfast becomes a lottery draw. His crumb, your crumb, in his notebook. A taste, a tune, a word, a face. He wakes knowing a knot nobody taught him. You wake saying sorry in a voice that isn't yours.
lines.say: [playful, quick, the list bouncing, then a shade stranger on the last sentence] Breakfast becomes a lottery draw. His crumb, your crumb, in his notebook. A taste, a tune, a word, a face. He wakes knowing a knot nobody taught him. You wake saying sorry in a voice that isn't yours.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So is a sleeping brain really working? About a hundred years ago a scientist said the experiment that won him a Nobel Prize came to him in a dream. He got up in the night and did it, on a frog's heart.
lines.say: [curious, then a storyteller's hush, the frog's heart with a small smile] So is a sleeping brain really working? About a hundred years ago a scientist said the experiment that won him a Nobel Prize came to him in a dream. He got up in the night and did it, on a frog's heart.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Sleeping brains do real work. Normally, you keep it.
lines.say: [plain, steady, the second sentence pointed] Sleeping brains do real work. Normally, you keep it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And you've rented yours before, for free. Those squiggly words you typed to prove you weren't a robot? One of those tests, reCAPTCHA, used them to read old newspapers and books that computers couldn't. More than a hundred million a day.
lines.say: [conspiratorial, amused, the number landing with a lift] And you've rented yours before, for free. Those squiggly words you typed to prove you weren't a robot? One of those tests, reCAPTCHA, used them to read old newspapers and books that computers couldn't. More than a hundred million a day.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Spare seconds, turned into machine work. The band makes the same bargain with your whole night.
lines.say: [low, exact, the second sentence slower] Spare seconds, turned into machine work. The band makes the same bargain with your whole night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But here's the problem. Problem one. Ninety dollars for eight hours. So what's twelve worth?
lines.say: [slow, a pause after problem, Problem one said as a heading, a stress on twelve] But here's the problem. Problem one. Ninety dollars for eight hours. So what's twelve worth?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You rent your nap on the bus. You wake at the end of the line with four dollars and a craving for pickles.
lines.say: [amused, deadpan on the pickles] You rent your nap on the bus. You wake at the end of the line with four dollars and a craving for pickles.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And you're not the only one counting. The nurse has a band under her cap now, so the clinic shuts at noon. Therefore your boss sees the jar on your desk, and opens a nap room at work. With a till.
lines.say: [quickening, one thing tipping the next, dry on the till] And you're not the only one counting. The nurse has a band under her cap now, so the clinic shuts at noon. Therefore your boss sees the jar on your desk, and opens a nap room at work. With a till.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Boss: Twenty per cent. Pillows are mine.
lines.say: [brisk, pleased with himself, no room for argument] Twenty per cent. Pillows are mine.
lines.speaker: Boss

lines.text: Therefore sleeping for money is a day job. So the couple across the street sleep in shifts, and their jar never stops. And the empty warehouse by the bridge fills with cots, and a clerk with a clipboard stands at its door.
lines.say: [building, matter-of-fact, a shade darker on the warehouse] Therefore sleeping for money is a day job. So the couple across the street sleep in shifts, and their jar never stops. And the empty warehouse by the bridge fills with cots, and a clerk with a clipboard stands at its door.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Therefore the grandmother next door, eleven hours a night, out-earns the whole street.
lines.say: [delighted, a grin in the voice] Therefore the grandmother next door, eleven hours a night, out-earns the whole street.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Grandmother: Finally.
lines.say: [smug, satisfied, decades of waiting in one word] Finally.
lines.speaker: Grandmother

lines.text: Therefore nobody buys coffee. The coffee shops close. The pillow shop stays open till midnight. And the whole city is in bed by seven.
lines.say: [the chain running out, amused, then quiet on the last sentence] Therefore nobody buys coffee. The coffee shops close. The pillow shop stays open till midnight. And the whole city is in bed by seven.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Ten hours a night. Then twelve. Your jar becomes a shelf of jars.
lines.say: [hushed, counting up, a little awed] Ten hours a night. Then twelve. Your jar becomes a shelf of jars.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So what did twelve hours cost? First your keys. Then your PIN, gone, at the cash machine. Then you walk past your own front door. Twice.
lines.say: [a turn, each loss its own beat, the last word flat] So what did twelve hours cost? First your keys. Then your PIN, gone, at the cash machine. Then you walk past your own front door. Twice.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: You live here.
lines.say: [gentle, half a joke, worried underneath] You live here.
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: You sold twelve hours of nothing. And the nothing was never empty. Sleep was never idle.
lines.say: [low, steady, the last sentence landing like a door shutting] You sold twelve hours of nothing. And the nothing was never empty. Sleep was never idle.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You thought you were selling spare time. There was no spare time.
lines.say: [quiet, close, the second sentence slower] You thought you were selling spare time. There was no spare time.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You spend about a third of your life asleep. A third. Did you think it was for nothing?
lines.say: [plain, then a challenge, almost gentle] You spend about a third of your life asleep. A third. Did you think it was for nothing?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: In mice, the spaces between brain cells open up by about sixty per cent during sleep, and the waste washes out faster. Sleep is when your brain takes the trash out. Yours hasn't in a month.
lines.say: [clear, a storyteller's wonder, then flat and close on the last sentence] In mice, the spaces between brain cells open up by about sixty per cent during sleep, and the waste washes out faster. Sleep is when your brain takes the trash out. Yours hasn't in a month.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: About a hundred years ago, in 1924, two people were tested, and they forgot less after sleeping than after the same hours awake. And in rats, the day's activity replays in sleep, faster than real time.
lines.say: [measured, curious, a lift on faster than real time] About a hundred years ago, in nineteen twenty-four, two people were tested, and they forgot less after sleeping than after the same hours awake. And in rats, the day's activity replays in sleep, faster than real time.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Your brain files your day at night, on fast forward. For a month, nothing's been filed.
lines.say: [quick on the first sentence, then slow, the weight landing] Your brain files your day at night, on fast forward. For a month, nothing's been filed.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Sleep was never nothing. It was the one shift you always worked for yourself.
lines.say: [warm, low, intimate, every word placed] Sleep was never nothing. It was the one shift you always worked for yourself.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You've slept twelve hours a night and you look like the boy who stayed awake for eleven days for a science fair in 1964, whose thinking began to suffer by the end. He skipped sleep. You sold it.
lines.say: [dry, a story told fast, then the two short sentences cold] You've slept twelve hours a night and you look like the boy who stayed awake for eleven days for a science fair in nineteen sixty-four, whose thinking began to suffer by the end. He skipped sleep. You sold it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Your brother stops laughing. He gets out the stamp.
lines.say: [quiet, tender, a small smile on the stamp] Your brother stops laughing. He gets out the stamp.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: Don't peel it.
lines.say: [mock-stern, fond, a smile held back] Don't peel it.
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: But here's the second problem. Problem two. It's your brain, only yours. Whatever you lose, you lose alone.
lines.say: [low, a pause after problem, Problem two as a heading, a stress on only yours and alone] But here's the second problem. Problem two. It's your brain, only yours. Whatever you lose, you lose alone.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And Saturday is his graduation.
lines.say: [soft, a warning the voice doesn't want to give] And Saturday is his graduation.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Saturday. The hall. Folding chairs. Your brother on the stage in a gown and his cap, and no band under it today.
lines.say: [warm, proud, a lift on no band] Saturday. The hall. Folding chairs. Your brother on the stage in a gown and his cap, and no band under it today.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The weekend rate triples. So that night, you take twelve hours.
lines.say: [matter-of-fact, a shadow under it] The weekend rate triples. So that night, you take twelve hours.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: What'd you get? Show me.
lines.say: [eager, bright, already reaching for the band] What'd you get? Show me.
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: Two hundred and seventy dollars. The best night yet. You show him the band. He shows you his phone.
lines.say: [bright on the number, then slowing, the last sentence quiet] Two hundred and seventy dollars. The best night yet. You show him the band. He shows you his phone.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: You cried. Remember?
lines.say: [small, hopeful, the smile fading on the second word] You cried. Remember?
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: You were there. You have the photo. You sold the night before your brain could file the day.
lines.say: [very quiet, close, no music in the voice] You were there. You have the photo. You sold the night before your brain could file the day.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But here's the third problem. Problem three. You weren't the only one who worked out the weekend rate. And the price is about to fall.
lines.say: [steady, Problem three as a heading, a pause before And the price, a stress on fall] But here's the third problem. Problem three. You weren't the only one who worked out the weekend rate. And the price is about to fall.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Ninety. Forty-one. Twelve. Everyone has a band on now.
lines.say: [slow, counting down, each number its own beat with a full pause after it] Ninety. ... Forty-one. ... Twelve. ... Everyone has a band on now.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It's true. The US is one of the few countries that lets companies pay people for plasma, and it supplies about two thirds of the world's. People cross that bridge from Mexico twice a week to sell theirs, because a day's work across the river pays about nine dollars. Now they cross to sleep.
lines.say: [plain, factual, a weight on it's true, the last sentence quiet and flat] It's true: the US is one of the few countries that lets companies pay people for plasma, and it supplies about two thirds of the world's. People cross that bridge from Mexico twice a week to sell theirs, because a day's work across the river pays about nine dollars. Now they cross to sleep.

lines.text: The warehouse by the bridge. A thousand sleepers in shifts, a thousand pale workers typing over them.
lines.say: [hushed, wide, a little horrified] The warehouse by the bridge. A thousand sleepers in shifts, a thousand pale workers typing over them.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: An eighteenth-century chess robot had a chess master hidden inside it. Amazon named a website after it, Mechanical Turk, and paid people a few cents a task. This is the human inside the machine. In bulk.
lines.say: [a storyteller's curiosity, then cold and clipped on the last two sentences] An eighteenth-century chess robot had a chess master hidden inside it. Amazon named a website after it, Mechanical Turk, and paid people a few cents a task. This is the human inside the machine. In bulk.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And the best-rested brains fetch the most. More than a third of American adults already don't get enough sleep. So the people who need the money most earn the least.
lines.say: [level, grim, the last sentence slow] And the best-rested brains fetch the most. More than a third of American adults already don't get enough sleep. So the people who need the money most earn the least.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It's true. The Kenyan workers who labelled data to train ChatGPT were paid less than two dollars an hour. The night is heading there.
lines.say: [plain, quiet anger held in, the last sentence flat] It's true. The Kenyan workers who labelled data to train ChatGPT were paid less than two dollars an hour. The night is heading there.

lines.text: Your brother, band on, at the warehouse door at midnight.
lines.say: [low, worried, watching from a distance] Your brother, band on, at the warehouse door at midnight.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Clerk: Rested ones only.
lines.say: [flat, blunt, crisp, a clear stress on rested] Rested ones only.
lines.speaker: Clerk

lines.text: So a night is worth twelve dollars, and he can't even sell that. But one offer hasn't fallen. The man in the grey suit comes back.
lines.say: [quiet, bitter on the first sentence, then low and slow: the turn] So a night is worth twelve dollars, and he can't even sell that. But one offer hasn't fallen. The man in the grey suit comes back.

lines.text: The kitchen table. A premium contract. Triple pay, every night, all night, for a year. It clears what the family owes by spring. And no more Thursdays in the chair.
lines.say: [low, tempted, the terms laid down one by one, the last sentence almost kind] The kitchen table. A premium contract. Triple pay, every night, all night, for a year. It clears what the family owes by spring. And no more Thursdays in the chair.

lines.text: Somebody has tried to buy the night before. Before the 2021 Super Bowl, America's biggest football night, a beer company ran a film meant to put its beer into people's dreams. About forty sleep and dream scientists signed an open letter against it.
lines.say: [dry, a raised eyebrow on the beer, then sober on the letter] Somebody has tried to buy the night before. Before the twenty twenty-one Super Bowl, America's biggest football night, a beer company ran a film meant to put its beer into people's dreams. About forty sleep and dream scientists signed an open letter against it.

lines.text: Sign, and nobody in this house sits in that chair again. Don't, and it's Thursday forever. You can't sleep on it. Sleeping is the job.
lines.say: [even, both sides given their full weight, the last two sentences slow and dry] Sign, and nobody in this house sits in that chair again. Don't, and it's Thursday forever. You can't sleep on it. Sleeping is the job.

lines.text: You pick up the pen.
lines.say: [quiet, clear, a small stress on pen] You pick up the pen.

lines.text: Brother: Not yet. Look.
lines.say: [urgent, low, a hand already down] Not yet. Look.

lines.text: Six weeks of crumbs, his and yours. He thinks they add up to something.
lines.say: [quiet, curious, leaning toward the notebook] Six weeks of crumbs, his and yours. He thinks they add up to something.

lines.text: Broker: Offer closes midnight.
lines.say: [cool, polite, a door closing in the voice] Offer closes midnight.

lines.text: The kitchen clock. Eleven.
lines.say: [flat, a tick in the voice] The kitchen clock. Eleven.

lines.text: The crumbs on the bed. His and yours.
lines.say: [hushed, close, a secret about to open] The crumbs on the bed. His and yours.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: He opens the laptop.
lines.say: [quiet, quick, a held breath] He opens the laptop.

lines.text: One brain, one band, one jar, the leaflet said. Each brain stays its own.
lines.say: [slow, the leaflet's words turned over and found wrong] One brain, one band, one jar, the leaflet said. Each brain stays its own.

lines.text: There was never one of anything. You never lost anything alone. For eight hours a night, every sleeper on the band was one mind.
lines.say: [slow, each sentence its own step with air between, a stress on never, on alone, on one mind] There was never one of anything. You never lost anything alone. For eight hours a night, every sleeper on the band was one mind.

lines.text: In 2020, over a million people lent their idle home computers to one project, and its scientists called the result the first computer to pass a billion billion sums a second. Spare machines, linked into one. Now spare brains.
lines.say: [wonder, building, then the last two fragments quiet and cold] In twenty twenty, over a million people lent their idle home computers to one project, and its scientists called the result the first computer to pass a billion billion sums a second. lines.text: So what's the job? The crumbs fit together. Into a drawing. And the drawing is a machine.
lines.say: [a whisper, a question, then each piece clicking into place] So what's the job? The crumbs fit together. Into a drawing. And the drawing is a machine.

lines.text: The job the sleepers are paid for is to design the thing that will never need sleepers.

lines.text: The biggest idea people ever had together, and nobody was awake for it.
lines.say: [quiet, almost tender, a line said once] The biggest idea people ever had together, and nobody was awake for it.

lines.text: Eleven fifty-eight. The pen in one hand. The band in the other, its teal light on.
lines.say: [tense, hushed, the clock in the voice] Eleven fifty-eight. The pen in one hand. The band in the other, its teal light on.

lines.text: The man in the grey suit, at midnight, for your answer. Nobody opens.
lines.say: [hushed, still, the last two words flat] The man in the grey suit, at midnight, for your answer. Nobody opens.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You lie down with nothing on your forehead. The offer's gone. And so is your way out of the chair.
lines.say: [soft, honest, no comfort offered] You lie down with nothing on your forehead. The offer's gone. And so is your way out of the chair.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And for the first time in six weeks, nobody's typing.
lines.say: [a whisper, relief in it, the room heard] And for the first time in six weeks, nobody's typing.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You wake. You know your street. You remember yesterday: his face over the notebook.
lines.say: [warm, slow, waking with the voice, a smile on his face] You wake. You know your street. You remember yesterday: his face over the notebook.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And one dream that was only yours. A bridge, in your own colours. Nobody else dreamt it.
lines.say: [tender, hushed, the last sentence almost proud] And one dream that was only yours. A bridge, in your own colours. Nobody else dreamt it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Brother: What'd you get, then?
lines.say: [gentle, teasing, already knowing the answer] What'd you get, then?
lines.speaker: Brother

lines.text: Tonight you'll lie down, and you'll be clocking in. You always were. The shift is yours.
lines.say: [warm, close, slow, the last three words placed like a hand on a shoulder] Tonight you'll lie down, and you'll be clocking in. You always were. The shift is yours.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Broker: This one's for daytime.
lines.say: [easy, smiling, the same salesman, a new box] This one's for daytime.
lines.speaker: Broker

lines.text: So, would you rent your nights? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
lines.say: [light, direct, a friend asking, the last sentence brisk] So, would you rent your nights? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
lines.speaker: narrator
